power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Stress is an umbrella concept that lacks a universally agreed upon definition.
The ambiguous conceptualization of stress undermines theoretical integration, construct validity, and cumulative knowledge development.

In our critical review, we delineate sources of conceptual ambiguity, describe obstacles in the operationalization and conceptualization of stress, and evaluate whether the term stress itself is necessary for scientific exploration.
We show that we do not need the term stress to describe the phenomena studied in stress research.
However, the term 'stress' may still be useful to refer to a field of research and to integrate research findings.
We demonstrate that phenomena related to stress can be described using more precise constructs: stressors, stress responses, and health outcomes.
To facilitate conceptual clarity, we synthesize umbrella definitions for these constructs.

Because these umbrella definitions remain necessarily broad, we emphasize that specifying the conceptualization and operationalization of the stressor, stress response, and health outcomes is indispensable for empirical rigor.
To that end, we introduce the Stress Conceptualization Checklist for Empirical Studies (SuCCES), a structured reporting framework.
The checklist covers formulation of the conceptualization, operationalization, differentiation, life period, assessment window, and context.
This reporting standard aims to strengthen construct validity, improve measurement coherence, and promote cumulative progress in research on stress-related processes.
"Stress, in addition to being itself and the result of itself, is also the cause of itself" Stress is an umbrella term that is used for a plethora of phenomena.
Almost forty years ago Pollock (1988) noted that "stress itself eludes definition, and there is no consensus as to what it encompasses".
text.formatted: Almost forty years ago <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Pollock (1988)</ref> noted that "stress itself eludes definition, and there is no consensus as to what it encompasses".

text.text: The status quo is not very different today.

Stress describes a variety of distinct components of a sequential process, with both internal and external causes of a stress response including physiological and psychological elements (Monroe, 2008; Monroe & Slavich, 2020).

text.text: Accordingly, stress theories have different foci, and conceptualized stress either as a stimulus, a response process, or as the interaction between the environment and a person (Aldwin, 2012; Hobfoll, 1989; Hutmacher, 2021; Mulhall, 1996), as we discuss below.

text.text: Such transactional theories typically build on the theory of stress and coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), which assumed that relationships between people and their environment are bidirectional and dynamic.

text.text: Stress became defined as a person's cognitive appraisal of the person-environment transaction, by weighting their resources to cope against the situational demands and the threat to wellbeing (Folkman et al., 1986; Lazarus & Folkman, 1984).

text.text: Psychological processes such as appraisals and coping may also reflect a stress response instead of a person-environment transaction, and some theorists therefore do not distinguish between stress responses and person-environment transactions (e.g., Epel et al., 2018; Myroniuk et al., 2026).

text.text: People are thought to experience stress when their phenotype does not match the environment in which they live now, compared to the environment they grew up in (i.e., low person-environment fit).

The concept of allostatic load similarly describes how identical external environments can produce highly heterogeneous biological configurations in different people based on their history, coping mechanisms, and genetic variations (McEwen, 2000).

text.text: To delineate how to deal with this conceptual ambiguity, it may be useful to reflect on plausible reasons for the unclear conceptualization of stress.
One historical reason for the lack of clarity of the stress concept is the problematic transfer of the term stress from the field of physics to the medical and social sciences.

The earliest scientifically rigorous mention of the term "stress" in physics defined stress as the directed reactive force distribution per unit area inside a material as a reaction to applied external force (Azadi, 2017; Cauchy, 1821).
text.formatted: The earliest scientifically rigorous mention of the term "stress" in physics defined stress as the directed reactive force distribution per unit area inside a material as a reaction to applied external force <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Azadi, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Cauchy, 1821)</ref>.

text.text: In this physics context, the other important measure is strain, which describes the amount of deformation as a result of stress (Kopin, 1995).
text.formatted: In this physics context, the other important measure is strain, which describes the amount of deformation as a result of stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Kopin, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: When stress vanishes, strain may also return to zero because of the elastic behavior of the material, and the object's shape restores completely once the source of deformation is removed.
However, when stress crosses a material-specific elasticity limit, the object may be permanently deformed, which indicates strain.

Because physicists view stress as a theoretical variable that is not directly measurable, they assess stress not by direct measurement but infer it from measurements of external force applied and strain.

The terms 'stress' and 'strain' were introduced into the medical sciences by Walter Cannon (1871 Cannon ( -1945) ) to explain the effects of stressors on human homeostasis; a regulatory mechanism to maintain bodily stability.

text.text: Similar to physicists, Cannon (1935) used the term stress mainly to explain external force to the body (i.e., the stimulus or "load"), such as change in temperature in the atmosphere, which could lead to strain in the biological system, and thus a failure to maintain homeostasis.

text.text: However, as described below, the term 'stress' was kept while the terms 'external force' (load) and 'strain' were often lost over the course of time.
An exception are theories in the occupational health literature in which strains have been defined as the outcomes of a stress process that was triggered by a stressor (Lepine et al., 2005).

text.text: Hans Selye (1907 Selye ( -1982) ) popularized the stress concept in the medical and social sciences, to explain the maladaptive effects of stimuli on the human body (for a more in depth discussion of the work of Hans Selye and Walter Cannon, see Cooper & Dewe, 2004; Hinkle, 1974; Kopin, 1995; Viner, 1999). Selye (1956) used the term 'stress response' to explain the state of the body after exposure to external stimuli.

text.text: He also coined 'stressor' to describe the agent or demand that evokes a stress response, which corresponds with the external force in physics.
Following Selye, researchers started to use the term stress to describe both the causal factors leading to a response in human beings as well as this non-specific stress response itself.
Selye's definition of stress can also explain why there are so many different operationalizations of stress (Kagan, 2016).

text.text: Although Selye used different definitions during his career, his most commonly used definition of stress is "the nonspecific response of the body to any demand", which captures a broad variety of variables (Selye, 1976).

text.text: In fact, Selye (1976) enumerated >150 stressors and ~100 manifestations of stress in his book Stress in Health and Disease. Selye's (1976) stressors and conditioning agents included exogenous stimuli (such as drugs, pollution, isolation, parachute jumping, shift work) and endogenous stimuli (such as grief, anxiety, cognition, sleep deprivation, and corticoids).

text.text: Moreover, Selye listed both physiological and psychological manifestations of stress, for example, alterations in the liver, learning, cognitions, memory, emotions, vitamin c levels, tumors, and appetite.
Interestingly, some hormones were recorded as both stressors and manifestation of stress (e.g., glucagon, insulin and corticoids).
Hence, Selye's stress definition makes almost any measure tapping into exposure, perception, emotion, or biological response a measurement of stress.
The term 'stress' may also be ambiguous because the use of the term has evolved over time in science and society.

text.text: A more philosophical reason for the lack of conceptual clarity is that the concept of stress is a human social construction (Pollock, 1988; Young, 1980).

Kagan (2016) noted that this lack of conceptual clarity is especially present among psychologists, who tend to "lump" abstract concepts without specifying the characteristics or participant responses.

text.text: Current stress conceptualizations do not meet all criteria for a good concept such as 'coherence' (a bounded set of phenomena) and 'differentiation' (from neighbouring concepts; see Gerring, 1999; MacKenzie, 2003; Suddaby, 2010).

text.text: Stress operationalizations across scientific disciplines, such early childhood events, cognitive appraisals, corticosteroids, neural regulation, and momentary emotional states, exemplify that there is a lack of coherence.
Furthermore, the lack of differentiation is exemplified by the fact that stress responses and the pathogenic effects of stress are difficult to distinguish (Tennant et al., 1985).

text.text: For example, heightened stress levels may be inferred from heightened cortisol levels, rumination, and restlessness, but these concepts are also elements of umbrella concepts like anxiety and depression.
Similarly, it may be hard to draw a conceptual line between some perceived stressful daily hassles, such as sleep problems and symptoms of psychopathology (Wright et al., 2020).

text.text: A related critique of some conceptualizations of stress is that they are tautological (MacKenzie, 2003; Podsakoff et al., 2016; Suddaby, 2010), such as Selye's (1976) definition of stressors and stress (Kagan, 2016; Rushen, 1986); a stress response is a response that is caused by a stressor, which is defined as something that is able to elicit a stress response.

text.text: Furthermore, when stressors are conceptually conflated with the stress response, they risk being confounded in measurement, and thereby threaten the validity of the research (Harkness & Monroe, 2016).

text.text: A more fundamental problem with the many conceptualizations of stress is exactly the diversity in phenomena and entities that have been labelled as stress.

A concise concept definition demands a specification of the exact properties of a phenomenon (e.g., whether these properties include perceptions or feelings), and the entity, that is the, the person, object, or context to which these properties apply (Podsakoff et al., 2016).

Koolhaas and colleagues (2011) proposed to restrict the use of stress to stressors that are uncontrollable and unpredictable, in order to distinguish these stressors from demands that fall within the adaptive capacity and normal physiological responses.

text.text: These examples illustrate that theories either strive to include or exclude 'normal' event or responses and that there, evidently, may be no consensus on a single universal definition of stress.
Can we describe stress research without using the term stress?
One radical way to deal with the ambiguity of the concept stress is to drop it, as many have suggested (e.g. Crosswell et al., 2022; Hinkle, 1974; Kagan, 2016; Rushen, 1986).

text.text: The question is whether we even need the term stress to describe the phenomena of interest in empirical stress research.
The answer is no because more specific terminology can be used to describe stress.
To illustrate, stressors be described as life-events, long-term difficulties, childhood trauma, or daily hassles.
Examples of more specific terms to describe work stress are performance constraints, conflicts with colleagues, interruptions at work, illegitimate tasks, and daily negative work events.

In the medical field, physiological indicators of functioning of the stress system have been examined, such as circulating plasma levels of Creactive protein (CRP) interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha as markers of the immune-inflammatory system, cortisol measures as markers of functioning of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-axis (HPA-axis), and indicators of heart rate, pre-ejection period, and respiratory sinus arrhythmia as markers of functioning of the autonomic nervous system (Black et al., 2017).

text.text: Evidently, the term stress is not needed to describe the aforementioned phenomena, that is, authors could directly describe the constructs they are measuring.
The only construct that is hard to measure without the word stress is the feeling of stress.

Feelings of stress have been measured by asking about how stressed someone has felt (e.g., Snippe et al., 2023) or how often someone felt stressed (Kuckuck et al., 2025), which is hard to measure in another way than by using the word 'stress'.

text.text: The provided examples of stress studies illustrate that the use of the term "stress" is not crucial to describe the phenomena we study.
Yet, stress became so deeply ingrained in everyday language and the scientific discourse that the term "stress" seems impossible to "undo."

Stress may best be used to describe an interdisciplinary research field that focuses on the explanation of individual and group differences in stress related processes, often with the aim to predict health outcomes.

The phenomena that have been studied in the name of 'stress' operate on multiple levels (e.g., physiological, emotional, societal, person, environment) and interact to produce the key features of what we may call "stress".
Cross-level findings may complement one another (Eronen, 2021), and help identify similarities (Epel et al., 2018).

text.text: Their framework first requires specifying the phenomenon to which a concept refers-that is, the property or set of properties the concept is intended to represent (e.g., intrinsic characteristics, cognitions, affective states, or perceptions).
Second, researchers must identify the entity (i.e., object or event) to which these properties apply, such as an individual, a relationship, or a broader social system.

Applying these principles, we undertook the following steps to develop a coherent conceptual definition (see Supplement for specific methods): (1) Identify potential attributes of the concept by collecting a representative set of definitions, (2) organize the potential attributes by theme and identify any necessary and sufficient or shared ones, (3) develop a preliminary definition of the concept, (4) refine the conceptual definition.
The collected non-exhaustive set of 'stress' definitions presented in the supplement yielded key attributes provided in Table 1 that were used to identify overarching themes.

text.text: The first theme is the 'type of entity', which refers the object to which the given properties of the 'stress' definitions apply.
The found entities are stimulus, responses, and consequences.
The second theme is the 'type of phenomenon', that is, the property the concept represents.

The retrieved phenomena include physiological, emotional, behavioral, and cognitive changes, including appraisals of whether the stimuli are threatening or harmful, unpleasant, demanding, challenging, depriving, damaging, unpredictable, uncontrollable, overwhelming, or whether one has the resource to cope with the stimuli.
The third theme are the 'effects of stimuli or responses' including adaptation, maladaptation, disorganization of behavior, and disequilibrium.

Based on the type of entities of the first theme, three distinct components of a sequential process of the stress process can be identified: stressors, stress responses, and health outcomes (i.e., "strain").
The attributes of Table 1 were organized according to these three stages of the stress process.

Furthermore, the use of the term strain in physics may be slightly different since it refers to deformations of material that may not reverse, while humans are more like programmable or adaptive; systems that can redistribute external force, adjust properties, incorporate feedback, seek support and thereby deliberately recover.
1) Stressors are internal or external stimuli that are perceived as threatening (e.g., harmful, challenging, uncontrollable, or unpredictable) in a given context.
2) Stress responses are dynamic changes in physiology, emotions, cognitions, and behavior elicited by a stressor.
3) Health outcomes are the longer lasting adverse or adaptive consequences of the individual's accumulated stress responses.
Even though the formulated umbrella definitions distinguish different phases of the stress process, the definitions lack the specificity needed to adequately define a phenomenon in empirical studies.

Therefore, researchers should use these umbrella definitions to clarify the part of the 'stress' process that they are investigating but should also further specify the foci of the stressor, stress response, or health outcomes in their empirical study.

To guide researchers in doing so, we drafted the Stress Conceptualization Checklist for Empirical Studies (SuCCES) (see Table 2), which empirical researchers could use to be more transparent about their conceptualization and operationalization of stress.

As a first step described in the SuCCES, the study should describe the conceptual framework and/or conceptual definition of the stressors, stress response, or health outcomes that underpin the study.
Second, researchers could use specifiers for the type of stressor, stress response, or health outcome that is studied.
How to do so, is exemplified by the field of research on 'love'.
Similar to stress, love is studied interdisciplinary (e.g., in the fields of history, theology, philosophy, and psychology).

Researchers have narrowed their conceptualizations of love by addressing, for example, Christian love (e.g., Sullivan-Dunbar, 2009), Arendt's conception of love (e.g., Gregory, 2001), or obsessive desire or Limerence (Bradbury et al., 2025).

text.text: A limitation of our critical review is that the suggested umbrella definitions of stressors, stress responses, and health outcomes are not based on existing theoretical stress models.
Theoretical models of 'stress' often go beyond an abstract 'stress' conceptualization and additionally specify concrete phenomena or processes that lead to stress.

A systematic examination of theoretical models on stress can provide a comprehensive overview of the real-life phenomena that have been studied in the name of stressors, stress responses, or health outcomes.
In addition, we acknowledge that using our umbrella definitions and SuCCES checklist is only a first step to improve agreement on stress concepts.
Further theoretical integration across disciplines, pre-registration, and inclusion of the SuCCES checklist within reporting guidelines would be important next steps.
Stress may refer to a multitude of stimuli, responses and consequences thereof.
Stress may reflect different phenomena, from life events to heart rate variability.
There are different historical and philosophical reasons for the ambiguous conceptualization of stress.
Even though we do not need the term stress to describe the phenomena studied in stress research, it may still be useful to use the term stress to refer to a field of research.
By unifying existing conceptual definitions of the stress process, we have provided broad conceptualizations of the three core stress components: stressor, stress response, and health outcomes.

We recommend that researchers follow our proposed checklist for empirical studies (SuCCES) and describe the conceptual framework, the conceptualization and type of stressor, stress response and health outcome, the operationalization and differentiation between stressor, stress response and outcome, and specify the life period, assessment window, and the context of their study.
